title: Cutting One Route at a Time

scenes.visual: Title card: Cutting One Route at a Time.

scenes.tts: Freezing and the pressure rise arrive together. Do they travel one route out of the amygdala, or two?
scenes.visual: The map from chapter one, with the freezing and pressure arrows highlighted and a question mark between them. Title card: Cutting one route at a time.
scenes.narration: Freezing and the pressure rise arrive together. Do they travel one route out of the amygdala, or two?

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty eight, Joseph Luh-DOO and his colleagues asked exactly that, in rats.
scenes.visual: Card: LeDoux, Iwata, Cicchetti and Reis, 1988.
scenes.caption: In 1988, Joseph LeDoux and his colleagues asked exactly that, in rats.
scenes.narration: In 1988, Joseph LeDoux and his colleagues asked exactly that, in rats.

scenes.tts: First they damaged one target of the central amygdala. Two weeks later they trained the rats, and the next day played the tone alone.
scenes.visual: Four steps light up in order: damage one target, recover two weeks, train, test the tone alone the next day.
scenes.narration: First they damaged one target of the central amygdala. Two weeks later they trained the rats, and the next day played the tone alone.

scenes.tts: In the same rats, they measured both responses: freezing, and the rise in blood pressure.
scenes.visual: Two icons side by side: a freezing rat and a pressure gauge.
scenes.narration: In the same rats, they measured both responses: freezing, and the rise in blood pressure.

scenes.tts: Picture two bars for each group. Intact rats that had the pairing show two tall bars.
scenes.visual: Two small panels side by side: freezing (% of tone) and pressure rise (mmHg). Each shows a tall bar for intact paired rats. Small label: invented numbers, laid out in the design of the 1988 study.
scenes.narration: Picture two bars for each group. Intact rats that had the pairing show two tall bars.

scenes.tts: Intact rats without the pairing show two short bars. That short pair is our baseline.
scenes.visual: In each panel a short bar appears for intact unpaired rats, with a dashed line at its height: 8% in the freezing panel, +3 mmHg in the pressure panel. Label: baseline.
scenes.narration: Intact rats without the pairing show two short bars. That short pair is our baseline.

scenes.tts: For these invented numbers, we assume the damage leaves the baseline alone, and that each score is the baseline plus a learned part. So the excess over the baseline estimates the learned response.
scenes.visual: In each panel the region between the baseline line and the tall bar is shaded and labelled: estimated learned response (assumes an unchanged baseline and an additive score).
scenes.narration: For these invented numbers, we assume the damage leaves the baseline alone, and that each score is the baseline plus a learned part. So the excess over the baseline estimates the learned response.

scenes.tts: Suppose both responses need the same route through these lateral hypothalamus neurons. What should damage there do to freezing?
scenes.visual: Question card over the chart: Do both responses need these lateral hypothalamus neurons? The lateral hypothalamus is highlighted on a small brain map.
scenes.narration: Suppose both responses need the same route through these lateral hypothalamus neurons. What should damage there do to freezing?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: If both responses needed those neurons, both would fall. They do not. The pressure rise falls almost to the baseline.
scenes.visual: Lateral hypothalamus group: the pressure bar drops to +4 mmHg, just above its +3 mmHg baseline line.
scenes.narration: If both responses needed those neurons, both would fall. They do not. The pressure rise falls almost to the baseline.

scenes.tts: Freezing stays almost at the top. So freezing does not need the lateral hypothalamus, but the pressure rise does.
scenes.visual: The freezing bar for the same group stays nearly as tall as in intact paired rats. Labels: almost all, almost none.
scenes.narration: Freezing stays almost at the top. So freezing does not need the lateral hypothalamus, but the pressure rise does.

scenes.tts: Now damage the caudal, or rear, periaqueductal gray instead. What do you expect this time?
scenes.visual: Question card, with the caudal periaqueductal gray highlighted in the midbrain and labelled caudal.
scenes.narration: Now damage the caudal, or rear, periaqueductal gray instead. What do you expect this time?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: The reverse. Freezing drops almost to the baseline, and the pressure rise survives.
scenes.visual: Caudal periaqueductal gray group: the freezing bar falls to 9%, just above its dashed 8% baseline; the pressure bar stays at +19 mmHg, almost as tall as the intact +20 mmHg bar.
scenes.narration: The reverse. Freezing drops almost to the baseline, and the pressure rise survives.

scenes.tts: Each kind of damage impairs one response and spares the other. That pattern is called a double dissociation.
scenes.visual: The two lesion groups side by side, mirror images, each with a small residue above baseline in the impaired response. Label: double dissociation.
scenes.narration: Each kind of damage impairs one response and spares the other. That pattern is called a double dissociation.

scenes.tts: It means different targets below one amygdala node contribute to different responses.
scenes.visual: The map returns, with arrows 1 and 2 drawn as separate lines from the central amygdala. Small label: separable contributions, simplified model.
scenes.narration: It means different targets below one amygdala node contribute to different responses.

scenes.tts: In the worked problem, damage to the central amygdala itself leaves neither learned response above the baseline, as a shared source predicts.
scenes.visual: Central amygdala group: the freezing bar at 6%, slightly below its dashed 8% baseline; the pressure bar at +3 mmHg, on its +3 mmHg baseline. Label: invented numbers; no learned response above baseline.
scenes.narration: In the worked problem, damage to the central amygdala itself leaves neither learned response above the baseline, as a shared source predicts.

scenes.tts: One detail matters. The caudal midbrain damage used ibotenic acid, a toxin that kills cell bodies but spares passing axons.
scenes.visual: Close-up: cell bodies fade while axons running through the region stay lit.
scenes.narration: One detail matters. The caudal midbrain damage used ibotenic acid, a toxin that kills cell bodies but spares passing axons.

scenes.tts: So the freezing loss points to neurons in the periaqueductal gray, not to cut fibres. The same toxin in the lateral hypothalamus impaired the pressure rise while sparing freezing.
scenes.visual: The caudal periaqueductal gray glows; the passing axons stay intact. Then the lateral hypothalamus glows the same way, beside the pressure gauge.
scenes.narration: So the freezing loss points to neurons in the periaqueductal gray, not to cut fibres. The same toxin in the lateral hypothalamus impaired the pressure rise while sparing freezing.

scenes.tts: This experiment finds the routes out of the amygdala. It says nothing yet about a feeling.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: Different targets contribute to different measured responses, below one amygdala node.
scenes.narration: This experiment finds the routes out of the amygdala. It says nothing yet about a feeling.

scenes.visual: End card with the takeaway line.
